abstract.text: This paper proposes a real-time approach for longterm inertial navigation based only on an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) for self-localizing wheeled robots. The approach builds upon two components: 1) a robust detector that uses recurrent deep neural networks to dynamically detect a variety of situations of interest, such as zero velocity or no lateral slip; and 2) a state-of-the-art Kalman filter which incorporates this knowledge as pseudo-measurements for localization. Evaluations on a publicly available car dataset demonstrates that the proposed scheme may achieve a final precision of 20 m for a 21 km long trajectory of a vehicle driving for over an hour, equipped with an IMU of moderate precision (the gyro drift rate is 10 deg/h). To our knowledge, this is the first paper which combines sophisticated deep learning techniques with state-ofthe-art filtering methods for pure inertial navigation on wheeled vehicles and as such opens up for novel data-driven inertial navigation techniques. Moreover, albeit taylored for IMU-only based localization, our method may be used as a component for self-localization of wheeled robots equipped with a more complete sensor suite.

sections.summary: Introduces RINS-W, an IMU-only long-term inertial navigation method for wheeled robots, combining a recurrent deep detector for motion profiles with an invariant extended Kalman filter. Positions the work against high-cost INS and low-cost MEMS drift, and reviews related work on IEKF, vehicle constraints, ZUPT, and deep learning for pedestrian inertial navigation, noting the gap for wheeled robots and larger IMU sequences.

sections.summary: Defines the 3D inertial navigation dynamics and the IMU measurement model with biases and noise, highlighting the severity of triple integration. Introduces four binary motion profiles—zero velocity, zero angular velocity, zero lateral velocity, and zero vertical velocity—chosen for wheeled vehicles with shock absorbers. Explains that zero velocity does not imply zero angular velocity, and separates profiles into zero-velocity constraints (bias/pitch/roll correction) and vehicle motion constraints (long-term accuracy).

sections.summary: Evaluates RINS-W on the complex urban LiDAR car dataset. Specifies implementation (four LSTMs, thresholds, 100 Hz filter, noise covariances), detector training (urban06–14, 100 km, thresholds, ADAM, dropout), and evaluation metrics (m-ATE, aligned m-ATE, final distance). On urban15–17 (40 km), RINS-W beats wheel odometry and on average beats odometry aided by a much more accurate fiber-optic gyro, with 20 m final error on the 73-min urban16 sequence. Discussion attributes performance to detector quality, side information, and IEKF, and shows the necessity of lateral/vertical updates on a no-stop sequence.

admission.original: This paper proposes a real-time approach for longterm inertial navigation based only on an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) for self-localizing wheeled robots. The approach builds upon two components: 1) a robust detector that uses recurrent deep neural networks to dynamically detect a variety of situations of interest, such as zero velocity or no lateral slip; and 2) a state-of-the-art Kalman filter which incorporates this knowledge as pseudo-measurements for localization. Evaluations on a publicly available car dataset demonstrates that the proposed scheme may achieve a final precision of 20 m for a 21 km long trajectory of a vehicle driving for over an hour, equipped with an IMU of moderate precision (the gyro drift rate is 10 deg/h). To our knowledge, this is the first paper which combines sophisticated deep learning techniques with state-ofthe-art filtering methods for pure inertial navigation on wheeled vehicles and as such opens up for novel data-driven inertial navigation techniques. Moreover, albeit taylored for IMU-only based localization, our method may be used as a component for self-localization of wheeled robots equipped with a more complete sensor suite.

abstract.text: Abstract—This paper proposes a real-time approach for longterm inertial navigation based only on an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) for self-localizing wheeled robots. The approach builds upon two components: 1) a robust detector that uses recurrent deep neural networks to dynamically detect a variety of situations of interest, such as zero velocity or no lateral slip; and 2) a state-of-the-art Kalman filter which incorporates this knowledge as pseudo-measurements for localization. Evaluations on a publicly available car dataset demonstrates that the proposed scheme may achieve a final precision of 20 m for a 21 km long trajectory of a vehicle driving for over an hour, equipped with an IMU of moderate precision (the gyro drift rate is 10 deg/h). To our knowledge, this is the first paper which combines sophisticated deep learning techniques with state-ofthe-art filtering methods for pure inertial navigation on wheeled vehicles and as such opens up for novel data-driven inertial navigation techniques. Moreover, albeit taylored for IMU-only based localization, our method may be used as a component for self-localization of wheeled robots equipped with a more complete sensor suite.

sections.summary: Introduces RINS-W, an IMU-only long-term inertial navigation method for wheeled robots, combining a recurrent deep detector for motion profiles with an invariant extended Kalman filter. Positions the work against high-cost INS and low-cost MEMS drift, and reviews related work on IEKF, vehicle constraints, ZUPT, and deep learning for pedestrian inertial navigation, noting the gap for wheeled robots and larger IMU sequences.

sections.summary: Defines the 3D inertial navigation dynamics and the IMU measurement model with biases and noise, highlighting the severity of triple integration. Introduces four binary motion profiles—zero velocity, zero angular velocity, zero lateral velocity, and zero vertical velocity—chosen for wheeled vehicles with shock absorbers. Explains that zero velocity does not imply zero angular velocity, and separates profiles into zero-velocity constraints (bias/pitch/roll correction) and vehicle motion constraints (long-term accuracy).

sections.summary: Evaluates RINS-W on the complex urban LiDAR car dataset. Specifies implementation (four LSTMs, thresholds, 100 Hz filter, noise covariances), detector training (urban06–14, 100 km, thresholds, ADAM, dropout), and evaluation metrics (m-ATE, aligned m-ATE, final distance). On urban15–17 (40 km), RINS-W beats wheel odometry and on average beats odometry aided by a much more accurate fiber-optic gyro, with 20 m final error on the 73-min urban16 sequence. Discussion attributes performance to detector quality, side information, and IEKF, and shows the necessity of lateral/vertical updates on a no-stop sequence.
